items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the uniform commercial code, the civil practice law and rules, the lien law, the general obligations law, the banking law, the general business law, the arts and cultural affairs law and the personal property law, in relation to making technical corrections to conform with revisions to the uniform commercial code; and to amend chapter 505 of the laws of 2014 amending the uniform commercial code relating to modernizing commercial law in New York state, in relation to making technical amendments thereto
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5502

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the uniform commercial code, the civil practice law and
rules, the lien law, the general obligations law, the banking law, the
general business law, the arts and cultural affairs law and the personal
property law, in relation to making technical corrections to conform
with revisions to the uniform commercial code; and to amend chapter 505
of the laws of 2014 amending the uniform commercial code relating to
modernizing commercial law in New York state, in relation to making
technical amendments thereto

PURPOSE:

Legislation was enacted in 2014 (Chapter 505) which modernized Articles
1, 7 and 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). This bill:

- makes some necessary technical amendments in several sections of law,

- improves certain filing processes under Article 9 of the UCC regarding
security interests in personal property; and

- clarifies the applicability of the amendments to Article 9 to trans-
actions which were entered into on or after the effective date of the
2014 law (i.e. December 17, 2014).

SUMMARY and JUSTIFICATION:

Sections 1 through 14 of the bill make technical corrections in several
state laws. These amendments renumber several cross-references to
sections of law within the Uniform Commercial Code. Chapter 505 of 2014
renumbered some sections of the Uniform Commercial Code. As a result,
amendments are needed in several other state laws to update and fix
these cross-references.

Sections 15 and 16 of the bill amend Sections 9-406 and 9-408 of the
Uniform Commercial Code. Current section 9-406 renders unenforceable an
anti-assignment term of a payment intangible or promissory note that
secures an obligation. By way of contrast, current section 9-408 permits
a sale of a payment intangible or promissory note notwithstanding an
anti-assignment term but does not require the account debtor or maker to
attorn to or otherwise recognize the buyer.  The Amendments clarify that
effectiveness of an anti-assignment term of a payment intangible or
promissory note in the case of a sale or other disposition of collateral
under section 9-610 or an acceptance of collateral under section 9-620
is governed by section 9406 and not by section 9-408.

Section 17 of the bill amends Section 9-516 of the UCC to provide that a
filing office will no longer be permitted to reject a financing state-
ment that fails to provide the type of organization of the debtor, the
jurisdiction of organization of the debtor, or the organizational iden-

tification number of the debtor or a statement that the debtor has none.
This information was not considered to be sufficiently useful in prac-
tice, and instead it often added cost and delay to the filing process.

Section 18 of the bill amends Section 9-518 of the UCC to change the
term "correction statement" as used in Article 9 to the more accurate
term "information statement." Under the amendments, an information
statement may, but need not, be filed by a secured party of record who
believes that an amendment or other record relating to the financing
statement of the secured party of record was filed by a person not enti-
tled to do so. Under current Article 9 a correction statement may be
filed only by the debtor.

Section 19 of the bill amends Section 9-521 of the UCC to provide that
filing offices shall accept written initial financing statements, adden-
dums and records which conform to the format set forth in the official
text promulgated by the American Law Institute and the National Confer-
ence of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws. Using this nationwide stan-
dard will help simplify the filing process and make it more cost-effi-
cient.

Section 20 of the bill amends the effective date of Chapter 505 of 2014
to clarify the applicability of the 2014 amendments to Article 9 of the
UCC as they relate to transactions which were entered into after the
effective date of such 2014 law (i.e. December 17, 2014).

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect on the same date as Chapter 505 of 2014 took
effect, and shall apply to transactions entered into on or after Decem-
ber 17, 2014

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5502A

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the uniform commercial code, the civil practice law
and rules, the lien law, the general obligations law, the banking law,
the general business law, the arts and cultural affairs law and the
personal property law, in relation to making technical corrections to
conform with revisions to the uniform commercial code; and to amend
chapter 505 of the laws of 2014 amending the uniform commercial code
relating to modernizing commercial law in New York state, in relation
to making technical amendments thereto

PURPOSE:

Legislation was enacted in 2014 (Chapter 505) which modernized
Articles 1, 7 and 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). This bill:

-makes some necessary technical amendments in several sections of law,
-improves certain filing processes under Article 9 of the UCC, which
governs security interests in personal property; and
-clarifies the applicability of the amendments to Article 9 to
transactions which were entered into on or after the effective date of
the 2014 law (i.e. December 17, 2014).

SUMMARY and JUSTIFICATION:

Sections 1 through 14 of the bill: these amendments make technical
corrections in several state laws by renumbering several
cross-references to the Uniform Commercial Code. Chapter 505 of 2014
had renumbered some sections of the UCC. As a result, technical
amendments are needed in several other state laws to update and fix
these cross-references.

Sections 15 and 16 of the bill: These sections amend Sections 9-406
and 9-408 of the Uniform Commercial Code to resolve an incongruity
between these two sections and clarify the law.

Currently, section 9-406(d) allows assignment of a payment intangible
or promissory note to secure an obligation, even if such payment
intangible or promissory note contains an anti-assignment provision.
Current section 9-406(e) specifies that this provision does not apply
to certain sales of a payment intangible or a promissory note,
although the intent was that the provision should apply to an
enforcement sale of the collateral. By way of contrast, current
section 9-408 permits a sale of a payment intangible or promissory
note notwithstanding an anti-assignment term but does not require the
account debtor or maker to enforce or otherwise recognize the buyer.
The failure to resolve the conflict between sections 9-406 and 9-408
results in uncertainty as to legal rights in contracts governed by New
York law.

The amendments in sections 15 and 16 clarify this matter by keeping in
place a policy that has been part of New York's enactment of Article 9
for a half-century while resolving the tension between old and new
provisions. The bill clarifies that effectiveness of an
anti-assignment term of a payment intangible or promissory note in the


case of an enforcement of the security interest (e.g., sale or
retention of the collateral in strict foreclosure) is governed by
section 9-406 and not by section 9-408 It should be noted that the new
language will not adversely affect the rights of consumers inasmuch as
anti-assignment clauses (the subject of sections 9-406 and 9-408) do
not exist in mortgage notes and other negotiable instruments, and are
not used in consumer debt.

Section 17 of the bill: This section updates the filing rules in Part
5 of Article 9 of the UCC in order to allow use of the new uniform
form of initial financing statement and amendment. Section 9-516 is
amended so that it no longer requires the debtor's type of
organization or jurisdiction on the face of its current financing
statement forms.

The Uniform Law Commission had polled offices of the secretaries of
state (among other parties) regarding this information. They learned
that not only was the information not useful, but that requiring such
information had the negative effect of adding cost and delay to the
filing process.

Section 18 of the bill: This section updates Section 9-518 of the UCC.
It provides that a statement may, but need not, be filed by a secured
party of record who believes that an amendment or other record
relating to the financing statement of the secured party of record was
filed by a person not entitled to do so. Under the current version of
New York's 9-518, such statement may be filed only by the debtor. This
amendment would allow any aggrieved person to make filings on the
record should such person believe an unauthorized filing was made
against him or her.

Section 19 of the bill: This section amends Section 9-521 of the UCC
to provide for use of the New UCC Financing Statements being used
nationwide In addition to the fact the current NY forms have fields
for information that is not useful, the New York UCCs do not contain
fields for the new information required by the amendments enacted by
Chapter 505 of 2014 to be included on the face of the form (e g.,
indication of collateral being held in a trust or administered by a
decedent's personal representative, indication that the financing
statement is subject to the transmitting utility rules.) Using this
nationwide standard will help simplify the filing process and make it
more cost-efficient.

Section 20 of the bill: This section amends the effective date of
Chapter 505 of 2014 to clarify the applicability of the 2014
amendments to Article 9 of the UCC as they relate to certain
transactions which were entered into after the effective date of such
2014 law (i.e. December 17, 2014).

Chapter 505 did not include a definition for "transaction" to help
parties understand when its amendments would apply. Because secured
transactions often have a lifespan of many years, transactions entered
into before the effective date of new legal rules can continue in
existence for many years after that effective date. This bill contains
a definition for "transaction" to provide clarification and certainty.
It provides that a transaction can include any amendment,
modification, supplement or restatement, if such action contains an


express provision that the parties intend it to be a "transaction"
under the Chapter 505 amendments. This will allow parties to avail
themselves of the benefits of the new legislation immediately.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect on the same date as Chapter 505 of 2014
took effect, and shall apply to transactions entered into on or after
December 17, 2014

summary: Relates to making certain technical corrections relating to the UCC revisions.
